title: Who else was in the room
lede: The crash took most of the first generation of game companies with it. The two that mattered afterwards were a cartridge publisher founded by Atari’s own programmers and a Japanese company that arrived in 1985.

blocks.title: Six companies, forty years on
blocks.subtitle: The companies that competed with Atari in 1982–86, and what became of each.

items.name: Atari
items.text: Loss for 1983 after a $323M profit in 1982. Sold in 1984; the name survives under Atari SA.[^6][^7][^21]

items.name: Mattel Electronics
items.text: Deficit for 1983 to October. Maker of the Intellivision and Atari’s main competitor in 1981. Out of the business by mid-1984.[^1][^5][^7]

items.name: Coleco
items.text: Filed for bankruptcy protection in 1988. Hasbro bought its main assets for $85M in 1989.[^31]

items.name: Commodore
items.text: Its price cuts under Jack Tramiel “buried Atari” in home computers, in the Times’s phrase. Tramiel then bought Atari.[^7]

items.name: Activision
items.text: Founded in 1979 by Atari programmers. Value of the Microsoft transaction announced in January 2022.[^26][^28]

items.name: Nintendo
items.text: Machines it hoped to sell in the U.S. in 1986, after a test of about 90,000 in New York the previous Christmas.[^9]

blocks.source: Figures as cited. Commodore’s later bankruptcy is general knowledge and is listed in the data notes.
The two columns are in different currencies and 44 years apart; they are shown side by side for scale, not as a like-for-like comparison.
